rationale: With the snapshot question closed, this turn inspects a different A2 surface that the same thread of work keeps touching: what happens to an already-dispatched leadership-verification future (VerifyLeader) when leadership is lost while replication goroutines still hold it. Source reading shows the completion ownership is single-threaded and idempotent, so a future that a replication goroutine re-notifies onto the shared verify channel after the leadership-lost cleanup is answered once by the cleanup and then rejected as ErrNotLeader in the follower/candidate state instead of being double-completed or leaking.

investigations.question: When leadership is lost while a VerifyLeader request is outstanding, can the resulting future be completed twice or left permanently unanswered, given that replication goroutines still hold it and notify it onto the shared verify channel after the leader loop has already responded to the pending set?
investigations.hypothesis: A pending verify future lives in two owners at once: the leader loop's notify set (responded with ErrLeadershipLost by the step-down cleanup) and each replication goroutine's notify map (a separate map, cleared by notifyAll at the end of an RPC). A goroutine that notifies after the cleanup therefore pushes the same future back onto the shared verifyCh, where the follower or candidate loop will respond to it a second time.
investigations.discriminator: Trace who may call respond on a verifyFuture and with what synchronisation, and what happens to a future that a replication goroutine re-notifies after the step-down cleanup: a defect requires two concurrent responders (a data race on the responded flag or a double send on the error channel) or a future that is never completed. If respond is reachable only from the main goroutine holding the run loop, and the second arrival is answered under the same stateless reject rule, the sequence is ordered and idempotent, and the apparent double completion is refuted.
limitations: Source-only: no execution and no race-detector run was requested, so this explains the ownership and ordering rather than observing a concurrent step-down.
The analysis covers verifyFuture completion paths in the captured revision; it says nothing about other future types or about respond callers added later.
The timing window in which a replication goroutine notifies after the cleanup was reasoned from the code, not measured.

knowledge.statement: A verifyFuture can be woken by only one notification (vote is guarded by the notify channel being non-nil and set to nil when it fires), and every respond path is idempotent through the deferError responded flag; vote(true) only notifies once the counted votes reach quorumSize, while vote(false) notifies immediately so the leader loop can step down when any peer reports a new leader.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to VerifyLeader/verifyFuture handling in the captured revision, including the quorumSize==0 dispatch sentinel and the follower/candidate paths that reject arrivals on the shared verify channel with ErrNotLeader.

knowledge.statement: On stepping down, the leader loop responds ErrLeadershipLost to every future still in its own notify set; replication goroutines keep their notify maps separate and only clear them through notifyAll at the end of a replication RPC, so a late notification can push an already-answered verify future back onto the shared verify channel, where the next non-leader loop answers it again through the idempotent respond path.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to leadership loss (step-down, shutdown, or state change out of Leader) with outstanding VerifyLeader requests; the arrivals are handled by whichever run loop is active when they are read.

interpretations.rationale: The apparent double completion is refuted by completion ownership and ordering. verifyLeader registers the future in the leader loop's notify set and in each replication goroutine's notify map, and the step-down cleanup responds ErrLeadershipLost to everything still in the leader's own set (raft.go:511-526). The replication maps are separate and are only cleared by notifyAll when an RPC finishes (replication.go:100-111), so a goroutine that finishes its heartbeat after the cleanup can still call vote on the same future; vote sends the future onto the shared verify channel and nils its notify channel under voteLock, so it wakes at most once (future.go:272-293). The critical point is who responds: respond is reachable only from the main run loop for this future type (the leader loop's verify branch, the follower and candidate reject branches, and the step-down cleanup), and all of those execute on the single main goroutine, so the cleanup's respond and any later rejection are sequentially ordered rather than concurrent. The second arrival is therefore a no-op: deferError.respond returns early once responded is set, and if it were reached first it would simply answer ErrNotLeader through the same idempotent path (future.go:94-131, raft.go:181-186). The result is that a VerifyLeader outstanding at leadership loss is answered exactly once - ErrLeadershipLost from the cleanup - and any late wake-up on the shared channel is swallowed by the responded flag instead of double-closing the error channel or blocking a sender. A worthwhile boundary follows from the same reading but is not a defect: because vote records a false reply immediately, the leader steps down and answers ErrNotLeader as soon as a single peer reports a new leader, and because votes are only counted from replies, a partition that silences peers leaves the request unanswered until a reply, shutdown or the caller's own timeout resolves it.
counterevidence: The strong form of the suspicion - two concurrent responders racing on the responded flag - requires a respond caller off the main goroutine, and the captured revision has none for verifyFuture: replication goroutines only call vote/notifyAll, which never respond.
The shared verify channel is buffered (api.go:568) so the late notification itself cannot block a replication goroutine.
limitations: Source-only: the ordering argument rests on respond being called exclusively from the main run loop in this revision; a race-detector execution of a concurrent step-down was not requested.
The unresolved-caller-timeout boundary (a verified request that never gets a peer reply) is described, not measured.
No behaviour of other future types or later revisions is claimed.
